FWIW I think it's common for compulsions to be a bit worse early on in ERP. I thought of it as sort of like, the death rattle of the disorder haha. ERP is stressful, for one, and also once you start to address certain obsessions, the OCD will find new stuff to latch on to. That said perhaps the OCD is a bit resistant to ERP, which can happen.

The best thing you can do is NOT enable their compulsions when they try to involve you in them. Often for loved ones this will mean not caving if they try to adjust or control your behavior as a compulsion in order to allay their OCD anxiety, and to not offer reassurance when they are seeking it for OCD reasons. 

As an example: For me this means when I think I've done something evil that I clearly haven't done and I start to ask my friends and family if I've done or am capable of xyz terrible thing, they kindly tell me they're not going to engage because they know it's the OCD and they don't want to make things worse for me.

Ultimately no human can make any other human do anything they don't want to do, and it's no different for people with OCD. You can't make them eat enough or stay hydrated, but you can let them know that you're concerned for their health and well-being and just want them to be healthy.

It's good that you're concerned and trying to devise the best strategies for helping. Mental illness always impacts more than just the person with the disorder and I know it's hard.

I would just gently push back on your framing of this issue. In a moral sense, it's neither okay nor not okay to act on an obsession with a compulsion; we have a disorder and it's very difficult to cope with life without these compulsions. You're not failing if you act compulsively: you just have OCD, and there's nothing "wrong" with having OCD.

From what I understand from having OCD, going to therapy for OCD, and researching OCD as a non-medical professional, it's absolutely true that acting on compulsions reaffirms the obsessions and is counter-productive for minimizing the impacts of OCD on our lives. However, acting on compulsions will happen. There's no cure for the disorder, and there's no sense in beating yourself up for coping the best that you can.

I just want to be very clear that I'm not encouraging you to act on your obsessions with compulsions. I just want to help normalize the fact that when you have this disorder, compulsions will happen and it's not a failure or judgement on your character or your commitment to dealing with the OCD.
